query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the concentration of passivating elements (Al and/or Si) in CrFeCoNiX alloys (relative to when X is Mn) promotes a rapid and uniform formation of a continuous, coherent α‐Al2O3 scale at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative/corrosive environments, thereby preventing the formation of unstable, cracking or spalling oxide layers.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a baseline composition where X is chosen to result in lower passivating element content (e.g., higher Mn content).
generation.intervention: Optimize composition by increasing the concentration of Al and/or Si relative to Mn to enhance the availability of passivating elements.
generation.conditions: Exposure at high temperature (above 900 °C) in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere (e.g., air or oxygen-containing environments).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent α‐Al2O3 layer that serves as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced Al/Si content increases the diffusion of these elements to the surface during high-temperature exposure, which leads to the rapid formation of a dense and uniform α‐Al2O3 scale. This scale provides effective barrier properties that slow down further oxidation and inhibits the propagation of oxide cracking/spallation that is more prevalent when Mn-dominated oxidation products form.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with optimized Al/Si content will exhibit lower oxidation weight gains and develop thin, coherent, and well-adhered α‐Al2O3 scales, whereas alloys deficient in these passivating elements (or containing a high proportion of Mn) will form thicker, heterogeneous, and unstable oxide layers that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys with insufficient Al/Si content (or with X = Mn) that tend to form non-protective, mixed oxide scales (e.g., Mn-rich oxides) which are unstable under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.boundary: Valid for alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state when exposed continuously to temperatures >900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres; behavior may vary if the alloy enters different phase regimes or under cyclic oxidation conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold concentrations of Al/Si required for consistent α‐Al2O3 scale formation are not well defined and may depend on the interplay of diffusion rates and competing elemental oxidations in the high-entropy matrix.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys: one with a baseline composition rich in Mn (and relatively low in Al/Si) and another where Mn is partially replaced by Al and/or Si to achieve a higher concentration of passivating elements. Subject both sets to a controlled high-temperature oxidation test at >900 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere for a fixed duration.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/TEM imaging of oxide scale morphology
XRD analysis to confirm the presence and phase purity of α‐Al2O3 or other oxide phases
Adhesion tests to evaluate spallation or cracking of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased Al/Si content fails to form a coherent, continuous α‐Al2O3 scale (i.e., shows similar or worse oxidation rates, heterogeneous oxide layers, and spallation behavior compared to the baseline alloy), then the hypothesis that compositional tuning toward higher passivating element concentration governs stable oxide scale formation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. The presence of Mn, known for its high mobility and low-energy oxide formation, can deplete Mn in the alloy, causing pore formation and accelerating oxide growth. Tradition

reading.lever: Optimize passivating element (Al/Si) concentration to promote rapid, uniform, continuous αAl2O3 scale formation.
reading.why: Compositional tuning, as shown in TiAl systems, can yield a stable protective oxide, addressing the oxide cracking/spallation limitation in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
